title: Analysis | CPM's Malappuram jinx: Why do leaders slip the moment they utter M-word
content: It is not the first time that remarks about Malappuram had put the CPM in trouble and forced its leaders to come up with bewildering excuses. In 2024, in an interview he gave to The Hindu as Chief Minister, Pinarayi Vijayan said there was a deliberate attempt to paint his government as anti-Muslim. As it turned out, like characters who end up speaking the opposite of what they intended, the proof Pinarayi offered for this conspiracy was widely understood as an insult of Malappuram. "When our government acts against Muslim extremist elements, these forces try to project we are acting against Muslims," Pinarayi said in the interview. "For example, 150 kg of gold and hawala money worth 123 crore were seized by the state police in the last five years from Malappuram district. This money is entering Kerala for anti-state and anti-national activities," he said. When it was realised that things had gone out of hand, the Chief Minister's Office said these were not the CM's words. The daily then put out a 'correction note' saying that the reference to Malappuram was inserted at the insistence of the PR agency that arranged the interview. Then, there was the then culture minister Saji Cherian's careless remarks, made right after the huge gains made by the UDF in the 2025 local body polls. "The politics of the Muslim League spreads communalism, and one only needs to look at the names of those who won in Malappuram and Kasaragod to understand whether communal polarisation exists," he said. Was it a Sangh Parivar leader talking, political opponents and even scholars wondered. When the backlash began, Cherian sounded wounded. He said his words were distorted and apologised to his "Muslim brothers" who had been unnecessarily hurt. Natesan's curse Interestingly, the CPM suffered the most not for the insensible comments of its leaders but for what was said about Malappuram by Vellapally Natesan, the general secretary of SNDP Yogam whose political wing BDJS was a BJP ally. At an SNDP Yogam convention at Nilambur in Malappuram in April 2025, Natesan said that the Muslim community had hijacked all sectors in the district that Ezhavas in the district had no choice but to beg for MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) work. "Do we even have a nursery school for our children here in Malappuram," he had asked rhetorically. The party itself has concluded that its timid response to Natesan's remarks had cost it dearly during the 2026 Assembly elections. "Though the state secretariat issued a statement condemning the anti-Muslim utterances of Vellappally Natesan, the state review self-critically notes that it was not a strong response. The statements made by some of our leaders about this controversy also contributed towards further alienation from the people," states the Review of Assembly Election Results adopted at the Central Committee meeting in July this year. Sting in the nest Now, when the party appears to be in rectification mode, former Ponnani MLA and one of CPM's tallest leaders in Malappuram, P Nandakumar, made a reference to the district that, at least to the party's political opponents, sounded like the CPM is in no mood to junk its political tactic of alienating the Muslim voter to lure the majority Hindus. "Malappuram district is a nest of religious fundamentalists and sectarian forces," Nandakumar said while speaking at the delegate meeting of the Malappuram Extended Committee in Ponnani on October 3. Widespread criticism forced CPM state secretary M V Govindan and Nandakumar himself to come out and clarify the next day. Interestingly, both gave fundamentally different explanations. Govindan said Nandakumar was speaking of Muslim League and Jamaat-e-Islami. Nandakumar, on the other hand, said he was speaking of both Muslim and Hindu fundamentalism. Govindan's Jamaat trap Govindan seemed stuck in a strategy that has proved to be a resounding failure in the 2026 Assembly polls...
